[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register a company (Pty Ltd) with ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC); director IDs are issued by Australian Business Registry Services (ABRS)).
A company is a separate legal entity, so you register it with ASIC to get an Australian Company Number (ACN) before it can trade. Every director must have a director ID before being appointed, and the company pays an annual review fee every year it stays registered.
Timeframe: About 15 minutes online once you have everything ready; confirmation usually within 2 business days if documents are complete and the fee is paid.
Cost: A$636 to register a proprietary company (from 1 July 2026), then a A$342 annual review fee each year. Director IDs are free.
Before you start: Make sure a company suits you: sole traders, partnerships and trusts do not register with ASIC as companies. A company has extra legal duties and ongoing costs.
Before you start: Every director must apply for their own director ID before they are appointed. It is free, done through ABRS, and you keep it for life even if you change companies.
Before you start: To apply for a director ID online you need a Digital ID such as myID with at least Standard identity strength, plus your ATO-held residential address and details from two verification documents (for example a notice of assessment). Giving your TFN is optional but speeds things up.
Before you start: Choose a name that shows legal status (for example 'Example Pty Ltd') and check it on ASIC's name availability search, or let ASIC use your ACN as the name.
Before you start: Decide your state or territory of registration, registered office address and principal place of business.
Before you start: Decide your internal rules: the replaceable rules in the Corporations Act 2001, your own constitution, or a mix.
Before you start: Work out the share structure and members. For each member you need name and address and written consent; for each director and secretary you need full name (including former names), home address, date and place of birth, and signed written consent to act, which you must keep.
Before you start: If the company will trade under a name other than its exact company name, it needs a separate business name registration.
Step 1: Each director gets a director ID. Every proposed director applies for their own director ID through ABRS before the company is registered. Online is fastest: sign in with myID (Standard or Strong), answer the identity questions and submit; your ID appears on screen. If you cannot get a myID with at least Standard strength, ABRS has other ways to apply depending on where you live. (time: Immediate online; cost: Free)
Step 2: Choose and check the company name. Check the name on ASIC's name availability search. You can optionally reserve a name for up to 2 months using ASIC Form 410 if you are not ready to register. (cost: Name reservation fee applies (amount not confirmed); form: Form 410 Application for reservation of a name)
Step 3: Prepare company details and consents. Prepare the registered office and principal place of business addresses, your rules (replaceable rules or constitution), share classes and numbers, member details and written consents, and each officeholder's details and signed consent to act.
Step 4: Register through the Business Registration Service. Apply to register the company (proprietary limited, public, or special purpose) in the Business Registration Service and pay the fee. You can add the company's ABN, GST, PAYG withholding and a business name in the same application. Some cases, such as hiding a residential address or an unlimited company, need a paper form or business service provider instead. (time: About 15 minutes; confirmation usually within 2 business days; cost: A$636 (proprietary company, from 1 July 2026); form: Business Registration Service)
Step 5: Receive your ACN, certificate and corporate key. The Business Registration Service emails the ACN and certificate of registration. ASIC posts the corporate key to the registered office; you need it to use ASIC's company officeholder portal. Show the company name wherever the company trades publicly, and put the name and ACN on required documents.
Step 6: Do the annual review every year. ASIC sends an annual statement after your review date (usually the registration anniversary). Check and update the company details, pass a solvency resolution, and pay the annual review fee. Keep company records and the share register up to date throughout the year. (time: Each year; late fees apply if not paid within 2 months of the review date; cost: A$342 (proprietary company, from 1 July 2026))
Fee: Register a proprietary company: A$636.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$611))
Fee: Annual review fee, proprietary company: A$342.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$329))
Fee: Director ID: A$0.00 (Free to apply)
Contact: ASIC: 1300 300 630, https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/contact-us
Contact: Australian Business Registry Services (director IDs): 13 62 50, https://www.abrs.gov.au/director-identification-number
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Watch out: Becoming a director without a director ID is an offence (60 penalty units). Applying for more than one director ID, or misrepresenting yours, can mean up to 1 year in prison.
Watch out: From 1 July 2027 companies must give their directors' IDs to ASIC.
Watch out: Late fees apply if the annual review fee is not paid within 2 months after the review date.
Watch out: Directors have legal duties under the Corporations Act 2001; understand them before you agree to act.
Watch out: A company name does not cover other trading names. Register a business name for any other name you trade under.
Watch out: Moving from sole trader to company means a new ABN for the company and transferring any business name.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Apply for an Australian Business Number (ABN) (Australian Business Register (ABR), administered by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) as part of Australian Business Registry Services).
An ABN is the 11-digit number that identifies your business to government and other businesses. It is free, and you need one to invoice properly, avoid having tax withheld from payments you receive, claim GST credits and get an .au domain name. You can only get one if you are carrying on, or starting, an enterprise.
Timeframe: Usually issued immediately at the end of the online application. If you get a reference number instead, the ABR aims to review it within 20 business days.
Cost: Free. Applying for an ABN through the Australian Government costs nothing; private websites that charge a fee are not required.
Before you start: Check you pass the entitlement test: you must be carrying on or starting an enterprise in Australia (or be a Corporations Act company). Signs of a business include significant commercial activity, an intention to make a profit shown by a business plan, repeated and systematic activity run in a business-like way, and relevant skill.
Before you start: You are not entitled to an ABN for work you do as an employee (including apprentices, trade assistants and labourers, even if it is called contracting), or for a hobby. An employer should not make an ABN a condition of employment.
Before you start: If you have not started trading yet, you should already have taken some start-up steps, such as advertising, setting up a website or social media, getting licences or insurance, leasing premises or equipment, giving quotes or applying for finance.
Before you start: Choose your business structure first (sole trader, partnership, company or trust). It changes what the application asks and which other registrations you need, and changing structure later can mean a new ABN.
Before you start: Have your tax file number (TFN) ready, plus the TFNs of any associates such as partners, directors or trustees. Being identifiable from your TFN speeds the application up.
Before you start: Have ready: the date you need the ABN from (no more than six months in the future), your entity's legal name, business address, postal address, email and phone, your main business activity, the physical locations you operate from, and your ACN if you are a company.
Before you start: Email addresses must be 5 to 200 characters with no spaces and must not begin with support@, sales@ or info@.
Before you start: If you use a registered tax or BAS agent, have their agent number so they can be an authorised contact.
Step 1: Confirm you are entitled to an ABN. Read the ABR entitlement guidance and make sure your activity is an enterprise, not employment or a hobby. Keep evidence (business plan, quotes, licences, insurance, lease, adviser correspondence) because the ABR can review your entitlement at any time and ask you to prove you started, or took steps to start, your business from the date on your application. Applying without entitlement can lead to prosecution.
Step 2: Gather the information the application asks for. Collect your TFN and associates' TFNs, the ABN start date, legal name, business and postal addresses, contact details, main business activity, business locations, any previous ABN, your ACN (companies), and your tax or BAS agent number if you use one. You can save a part-finished application, but missing details will likely delay your ABN.
Step 3: Apply online through the Business Registration Service. Use the Australian Government Business Registration Service at register.business.gov.au. In the same application you can also apply for a business name, GST, an Australian company, PAYG withholding, fringe benefits tax, luxury car tax, fuel tax credits and wine equalisation tax, so you only enter your details once. (time: Most applications are finished in one sitting; cost: Free; form: Business Registration Service)
Step 4: Read the outcome at the end of the form. If approved you get your 11-digit ABN on screen straight away; save or print the confirmation. If you get a reference number, the ABR needs to check your details and aims to review within 20 business days; check ABN Lookup and expect a confirmation letter within 14 days of approval. If refused, you get a refusal number and a letter within 14 days explaining why and your review rights. (time: Immediate, or up to 20 business days if reviewed)
Step 5: Keep your ABN details up to date. Update your ABN details within 28 days of becoming aware of a change. Cancel your ABN if you close or sell the business, stop operating in Australia, or change structure (for example sole trader to company, sole trader to partnership, or partnership to company), and apply for a new one for the new structure. (time: Within 28 days of a change)
Fee: ABN application: A$0.00 (Free through the Australian Business Register / Business Registration Service)
Contact: Australian Business Register (business information enquiries): 13 92 26, https://www.abr.gov.au/contact-us/contact-abr
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Contact: Translating and Interpreting Service (TIS National): 13 14 50, https://www.abr.gov.au/contact-us/contact-abr
Watch out: Applying for an ABN, registering for GST or claiming GST refunds when you are not entitled can lead to prosecution or criminal charges.
Watch out: An ABN does not replace your tax file number; you still need a TFN.
Watch out: If a business you work for insists you get an ABN but treats you like an employee, you are probably not entitled to one; check the employee or contractor rules first.
Watch out: Changing structure (for example sole trader to company) usually means cancelling the old ABN and getting a new one, and you may also need to update your business name with ASIC.
Watch out: Some private websites charge to lodge an ABN application. The government application is free.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register a business name with ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)).
If you trade under any name other than your own personal name (or your company's exact name), you must register it as a business name with ASIC. Registration is national, so one registration covers every state and territory, and you choose 1 or 3 years.
Timeframe: About 10 to 15 minutes online. Confirmation usually arrives within 2 business days if you pay by credit card, or 5 business days if you pay by BPAY, EFT or bank transfer.
Cost: A$47 for 1 year or A$108 for 3 years (fees from 1 July 2026).
Before you start: You must register a business name if you run a business in Australia and are not trading under your own name. You do not need one if you are a sole trader trading under only your first name and surname, a partnership trading under all partners' names, or a company trading under its exact company name.
Before you start: You need an ABN, or an ABN reference number if your ABN application is still being processed. You can apply for both together in the Business Registration Service.
Before you start: Check the name is free on ASIC's business names register: green means available, amber means ASIC will assess it after you apply, red means it is not available.
Before you start: Also check IP Australia's TM Checker. You cannot register a name that someone already holds as a business name or trade mark, and a registered business name does not give you exclusive rights to it.
Before you start: Have an address for service of documents (an Australian street address or PO Box) and a principal place of business (an Australian street address). Email and mobile are optional but email is where ASIC sends official notices and renewal reminders.
Before you start: For a joint venture, have each participant's ABN.
Step 1: Check name availability. Search ASIC's business names register (green, amber or red result) and IP Australia's TM Checker. If the name is close to an existing trade mark, choose another name or get advice, because the business name register does not protect you against a trade mark owner. (time: A few minutes; cost: Free)
Step 2: Get your ABN or ABN reference number. The business name must be held by an entity with an ABN. If you do not have one yet, apply for the ABN and the business name together in the Business Registration Service. (cost: Free; form: Business Registration Service)
Step 3: Apply and pay online. Apply through the Business Registration Service or ASIC's online business name registration. Choose a 1-year or 3-year period, enter your service and principal place of business addresses, and pay. Registration takes effect once the application is submitted and payment clears (up to 24 hours), and ASIC then emails your record of registration. (time: Usually within 2 business days (card) or 5 business days (BPAY, EFT, bank transfer); cost: A$47 (1 year) or A$108 (3 years); form: Business Registration Service)
Step 4: Keep your details current. Tell ASIC about changes to your registration details, usually within 28 days. If your business structure changes and you get a new ABN, the business name must be moved to the new holder. (time: Usually within 28 days of a change)
Step 5: Renew before it lapses. ASIC emails a renewal notice at least 30 days before your renewal date. Renew online through ASIC Connect or 'Pay now'. If you hold several business names or a company, you can ask ASIC to align renewal dates. If you do not renew on time, ASIC may cancel the name and someone else could register it. (time: Notice arrives at least 30 days before renewal; cost: A$47 (1 year) or A$108 (3 years))
Fee: Register or renew a business name for 1 year: A$47.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$45))
Fee: Register or renew a business name for 3 years: A$108.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$104))
Contact: ASIC: 1300 300 630, https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/contact-us
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Watch out: Trading under an unregistered business name is not allowed if the name is not your own name.
Watch out: A registered business name gives you no exclusive rights. Only a registered trade mark does.
Watch out: If you miss renewal, ASIC may cancel the name and it can become available to others.
Watch out: ASIC publishes warnings about scams impersonating ASIC. Renew only through ASIC Connect or ASIC's own payment links.
Watch out: Business names are registered nationally; you do not register again with your state or territory.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register for GST (Australian Taxation Office (ATO)).
Goods and services tax (GST) is a 10% tax you add to most sales once registered. You must register within 21 days once your GST turnover reaches A$75,000 (A$150,000 for non-profits), or from day one if you provide taxi, limousine or ride-sourcing travel. Registration is free.
Timeframe: Register within 21 days of becoming required to. Check your turnover every month.
Cost: The ATO lists no fee to register for GST.
Before you start: You need an ABN first, or apply for GST at the same time as your ABN in the Business Registration Service.
Before you start: You must register if your current or projected GST turnover is A$75,000 or more (A$150,000 or more for non-profit organisations). If you are new and expect to reach the threshold in your first year, register now.
Before you start: You must register regardless of turnover if you provide taxi or limousine travel for passengers, including ride-sourcing, and whether you own, lease or rent the vehicle.
Before you start: You also need GST registration if you want to claim fuel tax credits.
Before you start: The ATO says people earning through the sharing economy or digital platforms may also need to register; check the ATO's sharing economy guidance for your activity.
Before you start: GST turnover is your total business income (not profit), minus GST in your sales, certain sales to associates, input-taxed sales, sales not connected with an enterprise, and sales not connected with Australia. Current turnover is this month plus the previous 11; projected turnover is this month plus the next 11.
Before you start: If you register voluntarily, you generally must stay registered for at least 12 months.
Step 1: Work out your GST turnover. Calculate current GST turnover (this month and the previous 11 months) and projected GST turnover (this month and the next 11). Leave out sales of business assets and sales made only because you are closing or substantially reducing the business. Repeat this check monthly. (time: Monthly)
Step 2: Register. Register through the Business Registration Service (with or after your ABN), ATO Online services for business, your registered tax or BAS agent, or by phoning the ATO business enquiries line. Choose the date your registration starts. (time: Within 21 days of reaching the threshold; cost: No fee listed; form: Business Registration Service)
Step 3: Set up your prices, invoices and records. Once registered, include GST in your prices for taxable sales, issue tax invoices, and keep records so you can claim GST credits on business purchases.
Step 4: Report and pay GST on your BAS. Most businesses under A$20 million GST turnover report quarterly on a business activity statement (BAS). You must report monthly if GST turnover is A$20 million or more. If you registered voluntarily with turnover under A$75,000 (A$150,000 non-profit), you can report annually. You can also elect to pay quarterly GST instalments and report actual GST once a year. (time: Quarterly for most small businesses)
Contact: ATO business enquiries: 13 28 66, https://www.ato.gov.au/about-ato/contact-us
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Watch out: If you should have registered but did not, you may have to pay the GST on past sales out of your own pocket, plus penalties and interest.
Watch out: Taxi and ride-sourcing drivers must register before their first trip, even with very low income.
Watch out: Backdating is possible but generally limited to 4 years (unless there is fraud or evasion). Ask by phoning the business enquiries line.
Watch out: Voluntary registration generally locks you in for at least 12 months.
Watch out: Claiming GST refunds when not entitled to an ABN or GST registration can lead to prosecution.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-12; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register for payroll tax in Queensland (Queensland Revenue Office).
You must register with the Queensland Revenue Office (QRO) for payroll tax if you pay Queensland wages and your Australian taxable wages (or your group's) exceed $25,000 in a week; register within 7 days after the end of the first month that happens. Tax is payable on annual Australian wages over the $1.3 million threshold, at 4.75% (wages up to $6.5 million) or 4.95% (above), and employers with Australian wages over $10 million also pay the mental health levy. You register through QRO Online, lodge monthly returns by the 7th of the following month, and lodge an annual reconciliation by 21 July.
Timeframe: Register within 7 days after the end of the first month your Australian wages exceed $25,000 a week. Monthly returns are due 7 days after each month; the annual return by 21 July.
Cost: No registration fee. Payroll tax of 4.75% (or 4.95% over $6.5 million) on wages above the $1.3 million threshold, with the deduction phasing out by $10.4 million. Mental health levy of 0.25% on Queensland wages over $10 million, plus 0.5% over $100 million.
Before you start: Work out your Australian taxable wages for the month, including wages, super contributions, fringe benefits and some contractor payments, and those of any related businesses in your group.
Before you start: Grouping rules can combine businesses with common ownership or shared staff; the group shares one threshold.
Before you start: Each person using QRO Online needs their own individual account; you cannot set up a generic company login.
Before you start: Have ready: ABN, business and contact details, Queensland and interstate taxable wages to date, the date you first employed in Queensland and interstate, and the previous five years of wages.
Before you start: A tax agent or representative can register for you if authorised.
Step 1: Check if you need to register. Register if you pay taxable wages in Queensland (or are in a group that does) and your Australian taxable wages, or your group's, exceed $25,000 a week. You must register even if you expect total Australian wages for the year to stay under $1.3 million.
Step 2: Register online. Log in to QRO Online, choose Registration, then the payroll tax registration form, and search by ABN. Complete identification, business, contact, employment and wages details and the declaration, then submit. A submitted form cannot be edited. You are not penalised for the time QRO takes to process it. (time: Within 7 days after the end of the first month you exceed $25,000 a week)
Step 3: Calculate tax each month. Tax applies to wages above your deduction. The maximum monthly deduction is $108,333; above that it reduces by $1 for every $7 of wages, reaching zero at $866,666 a month ($10.4 million a year). The rate is 4.75% if annual Australian wages are $6.5 million or less, otherwise 4.95%. Eligible regional employers may get a 1% rate discount until 30 June 2030.
Step 4: Lodge and pay monthly returns. Lodge a periodic return and pay through QRO Online 7 days after the end of each month, moving to the next business day for weekends and holidays. In 2026-27 the dates include 9 November 2026 (October), 14 January 2027 (December) and 8 February 2027 (January). There is no June periodic return. (time: 7 days after each month)
Step 5: Lodge the annual reconciliation. Lodge the annual return by 21 July, which covers June wages and reconciles the year's deduction and any mental health levy. The 2026-27 annual return is due 21 July 2027. Some smaller employers lodge half-yearly (July to December due 14 January), with the second half in the annual return. (time: By 21 July each year)
Step 6: Mental health levy (large employers). If your annual Australian taxable wages (or your group's) exceed $10 million, a levy of 0.25% applies proportionately to Queensland taxable wages above the threshold, plus an extra 0.5% above $100 million. It is reported and paid with your payroll tax returns.
Step 7: Keep registration up to date. Update QRO when your business details, grouping or wages change, and lodge a final return if you stop paying Queensland wages. If you employ for only part of a year, the threshold is prorated by the days you paid wages.
Fee: Registration: Free
Fee: Payroll tax rate, Australian wages up to $6.5 million: See rate: 4.75% (On wages above the deduction)
Fee: Payroll tax rate, Australian wages over $6.5 million: See rate: 4.95%
Fee: Annual threshold: $1,300,000 (Maximum monthly deduction $108,333; deduction is nil at $10.4 million a year)
Fee: Mental health levy, Australian wages over $10 million: See rate: 0.25% (On Queensland wages above the threshold)
Fee: Mental health levy, Australian wages over $100 million: See rate: additional 0.5%
Contact: Queensland Revenue Office: 1300 300 734, https://qro.qld.gov.au/contact-qro/

Watch out: Grouping can pull related businesses together, so check whether your entities form a group.
Watch out: Interstate wages count toward the threshold and rate even though only Queensland wages are taxed in Queensland.
Watch out: Contractor payments can be taxable wages under the relevant contract provisions.
Watch out: Late lodgement or payment can attract interest and penalties.

In Queensland your council's planning scheme decides whether a proposal (a new use, a subdivision, operational work or some building work) is accepted development that needs no approval, or assessable development that needs a development permit through code or impact assessment. If it is assessable, you lodge a properly made application on DA Form 1 (plus DA Form 2 for building work) with the assessment manager, usually the council, and refer it to SARA or other referral agencies if the Planning Regulation 2017 requires. Impact assessable applications must be publicly notified. The council then has a decision period of up to 35 business days, and you can appeal the decision within 20 business days.

Statutory parts: application up to 30 business days, referral up to 30, public notification up to 60, decision up to 35 business days, each excluding extensions and time you take to respond.
Cost: Set by each council. Example Brisbane 2026-27 fees: new dwelling house material change of use $2,400; reconfiguring a lot into 2 lots $4,500; impact assessment adds $750 (domestic) to $17,100 (multiple dwellings). SARA referral fees, the QLeave levy on work over $150,000 and infrastructure charges can apply on top.
Before you start: Look up your property in your council's planning scheme (for Brisbane, City Plan 2014 online). Find the zone, any neighbourhood plan and overlays, then read the tables of assessment (Part 5 in most schemes) to see if your proposal is accepted, code assessable or impact assessable.
Before you start: Accepted development needs no development approval but must still meet any listed requirements. Prohibited development cannot be approved.
Before you start: Work out which type of development you have: material change of use, reconfiguring a lot, operational work or building work. One application can cover several.
Before you start: Check whether a state interest is involved (for example a state-controlled road, state heritage place, coastal area or protected vegetation). The SARA interactive mapping (DAMS) helps identify referral triggers. Identifying referrals is your responsibility.
Before you start: You need the owner's written, dated consent if you are not the owner.
Before you start: Consider a pre-lodgement meeting. Brisbane City Council charges $1,200 for one (2026-27); SARA offers pre-lodgement advice for state matters.
Before you start: For complex or impact assessable proposals, a town planner usually prepares the planning report and code responses.
Step 1: Confirm the level of assessment. Use your council's online planning scheme to check the zone, neighbourhood plan and overlays for the lot, then the table of assessment for your use or work. Where a higher level applies under an overlay or neighbourhood plan, the higher level wins. Code assessable development is assessed only against the scheme's codes and is not publicly notified. Impact assessable development is assessed against the whole scheme and must be publicly notified.
Step 2: Get pre-lodgement advice (optional). Ask the council's planning information line or book a pre-lodgement meeting to check the approach before you spend on reports. If a state matter is involved, contact the SARA regional office for your area. (cost: Example: $1,200 Brisbane pre-lodgement meeting (2026-27))
Step 3: Prepare a properly made application. Complete DA Form 1 (development application details) for material change of use, reconfiguring a lot and operational work, and DA Form 2 for any building work. Attach owner's consent, plans, a planning report responding to each applicable code, any specialist reports and the fee. In Part 6 of DA Form 1 you can say you do not want an information request if you are confident the application is complete. If operational or building work will cost $150,000 or more (excluding GST), pay the QLeave levy (0.575%) and attach the receipt; council cannot issue the permit until it is paid. (form: DA Form 1 Development application details)
Step 4: Lodge with the assessment manager. For most applications the assessment manager is the council: lodge online through the council's portal (Brisbane uses its online development application lodgement form and Development.i tracking). Paper or emailed lodgements can attract a scanning fee. Where SARA is the assessment manager, or when you refer to SARA, use the state's MyDAS2 online system to prepare and lodge. (cost: Council fee; Brisbane charges $300 to scan hardcopy lodgements)
Step 5: Application part: action or confirmation notice. If the application is not properly made, the council issues an action notice and you have 20 business days to fix it (in Brisbane, unpaid fees after an action notice mean the application is closed). Once properly made, the council issues a confirmation notice within 10 business days, saying what referrals and public notification apply. For code assessment with nothing else needed, a confirmation notice is optional. (time: Confirmation notice within 10 business days; application part up to 30 business days)
Step 6: Refer to SARA and any other referral agencies. If the Planning Regulation 2017 (schedule 10) triggers a referral, give the application and confirmation notice to each referral agency within 10 business days of receiving the confirmation notice and pay their fee. Concurrence agencies can require conditions or refusal; advice agencies only give advice. Referral agencies generally have 25 business days to respond. (time: Up to 30 business days for the referral part)
Step 7: Answer any information request. The council or a referral agency may ask for more information. You have 3 months to respond, which can be extended by agreement. The clock on the next part does not start until you respond.

For impact assessable applications (and those with a variation request) you must put a notice sign on the land, send a notice to owners of adjoining lots and publish a notice in a local newspaper or approved alternative. You (or your builder) engage a private certifier, who assesses plans lodged with DA Form 2, gets any council referral, issues the approval, inspects the work at set stages and issues a Form 21 final inspection certificate. Contracted work over $3,300 needs QBCC home warranty insurance, and owner-builder work over $11,000 needs a QBCC owner-builder permit before approval.

Before you start: Choose and check a certifier on the QBCC licence register. Your builder often engages them, but you can appoint one directly.

Before you start: Have plans, a site plan, soil test and engineering (footings, slab, framing, tie-downs) ready; the certifier relies on design certificates such as Form 15 from engineers.
Step 1: Confirm approval is needed. Compare your project with the exemption limits and your council's building approval fact sheet. If in doubt, ask a private building certifier; assessable work such as a dwelling, extension, patio, shed or carport over 10 m2, demolition or a pool needs approval.

You then need a unique vessel identifier (UVI), a certificate of operation and usually a certificate of survey from AMSA, plus crew with the right qualifications. (form: AMSA application for a certificate of operation)
Step 2: Find out which category of waters you will use. NT waters are inland, intermediate or open. Sheltered (smooth) waters are part of intermediate waters; around Darwin they are all waters landward of a line from about Lee Point to Charles Point. Use the categories of waters page and its interactive map to check your trip.
Step 3: Fit the minimum safety equipment. All waters: a lifejacket (PFD) for each person, an anchor with at least 3 m of chain and 50 m of rope, two paddles or oars with rowlocks for boats under 5 m without auxiliary propulsion, a bailer with lanyard or a bilge pump (pump needed if the bilge is covered), 2 litres of drinking water per person and a waterproof torch. Intermediate and open waters add two red flares, two orange smoke signals, a V distress sheet, and a fire extinguisher for boats 5 m and over. Open waters add a compass or working GPS, a chart of the area, a lifebuoy (over 10 m) and a registered EPIRB.
Step 4: Get the right lifejackets. Inland waters need a level 50 PFD or higher for each person; intermediate and open waters need level 100 or higher. PFDs must meet AS 4758 and inflatable ones must be serviced as the maker says. People on personal watercraft, small sailing boats (under 5 m or closed hull) and anyone being towed must wear a PFD.
Step 5: Register your EPIRB with AMSA. A 406 MHz EPIRB must be carried outside sheltered waters and more than 2 nautical miles from the coast. Register it with AMSA (free) and keep it in date; an expired EPIRB does not count. (cost: Free)

Riders and passengers must wear PFDs. Fines are 20 penalty units for an individual and 100 for a business without a lanyard.
Step 7: Learn the speed and distance rules. No more than 5 knots within 30 m of a swimmer, within 150 m of the waterline at Nightcliff, Fannie Bay and Mindil beaches, in a mooring area, within 30 m of a moored vessel, or within 100 m of a jetty, wharf or commercial shipping area. Do not make wash that endangers people, boats or structures, and keep at least 50 m from a water skier and the towing boat.
Step 8: Follow Darwin Harbour and harbourmaster rules. Do not anchor in shipping channels except in an emergency, do not tie up to navigation buoys, and keep clear of ships manoeuvring or leaving a berth. In the Port of Darwin, vessels under 25 m must give way to a ship flying flag H (pilot on board). Check notices to mariners and the regional harbourmaster's directions before you go.
Step 9: Get a permit if you want your own buoy mooring in Darwin. A permit is needed to install a buoy mooring for a recreational or commercial vessel in Darwin. Read the Darwin buoy mooring standards, complete the mooring permit application and email it to the regional harbourmaster. Permits last 4 years; renew between 30 and 7 days before expiry. (time: Permit valid 4 years; form: Apply for a mooring permit (Darwin))
Step 10: Check your gear before every trip. Make sure equipment is in good condition, meets the regulation standard and can be reached immediately. Flares, smoke signals, extinguishers and EPIRBs have expiry dates. Boating inspectors and police can board and issue infringement notices.

Every bond for a Victorian rental is held by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA), not by you or your agent. The bond is usually at most one month's rent. You register for RTBA online, start the lodgement, and each renter accepts it by email. If you receive the money, you must lodge it within 14 days. The renter can instead pay the RTBA directly or transfer a portable bond.
Timeframe: Lodge within 14 days of receiving the bond. Renters have 14 days to accept; lodgement usually completes in one business day.
Cost: No lodgement fee was published on the pages read. The bond is usually at most one month's rent.
Before you start: Work out the bond: no more than one month's rent unless the rent is over $900 a week or VCAT allows more.
Before you start: Each renter needs their own email address and a mobile number to pass Service Victoria identity checks.
Before you start: Decide who pays: you (from money the renter gave you), the renter directly, or a portable bond transfer.
Before you start: If the renter will pay the RTBA directly, they must tell you in writing before you start the lodgement.
Step 1: Register for RTBA online. Create a rental provider account. Add your bank details if the RTBA is to debit the bond from your account. (form: RTBA rental provider registration)
Step 2: Start the lodgement. Enter the bond amount, property address and each renter's contact details. On the funding page choose 'Rental provider' if you hold the money, or choose renter payment or a portable bond. (time: Within 14 days of receiving the bond)
Step 3: Renters accept. Each renter gets an email link to review and accept. If they don't accept within 14 days the lodgement lapses and you can restart it with the same details. (time: 14 days)
Step 4: Payment and receipt. The RTBA debits your account, or the renter pays by BPAY, direct debit or card (the link lasts 48 hours). The RTBA sends receipts with the bond number to every renter within 7 days; ask if you want one. If nothing arrives within 15 days, call the RTBA. (time: Usually one business day; payments can take up to 8 days)
Step 5: Manage and claim. Use your account to accept change requests within 14 days, update details or cancel. At the end of the tenancy, tell the renter in advance if you will claim on the bond (from 13 October 2026), and make the claim through RTBA online. Disputes go to VCAT.
Fee: Maximum bond: Varies: one month's rent (Unless rent is over $900 a week or VCAT approves more)
Contact: Residential Tenancies Bond Authority: 1300 137 164, https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/renting/rent-bond-bills-and-condition-reports/bond/rtba-enquiries-form
Watch out: Lodging late or keeping the bond yourself breaches the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.
Watch out: Only one renter can make the payment, so renters should agree who pays.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-12; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Lodging a rental bond with the Rental Deposit Authority in Tasmania (Rental Deposit Authority).
Every Tasmanian rental bond is held by the Rental Deposit Authority, not by you. You start the lodgement in Tasmanian MyBond using the Tasmanian bond lodgement form, and the tenant pays the Authority directly. The bond can be up to 4 weeks' rent; pet bonds aren't allowed. Taking the bond yourself is illegal.
Timeframe: Lodge before the tenant moves in so they can pay. Agents must lodge bonds paid to them within 10 working days.
Cost: No lodgement fee is listed. The bond itself is up to 4 weeks' rent, and no interest is paid.
Before you start: Register as an owner in MyBond and get your Owner ID (from Service Tasmania, or email rda@justice.tas.gov.au).
Before you start: Have the tenant's MyBond Tenant ID, email or mobile number.
Before you start: Have the tenancy start and end dates, weekly rent, bedrooms and address.
Before you start: Prepare the Tasmanian residential tenancy condition report at the same time: you must give it to the tenant if you take a bond.
Step 1: Sign in to MyBond. Sign in to Tasmanian MyBond as an owner, or register first. (form: MyBond)
Step 2: Complete the bond lodgement. Find or create the tenant, then fill in the Tasmanian bond lodgement form: tenancy dates, weekly rent, total bond (no more than 4 times the weekly rent), premises details and each contribution. Submit it so it reaches Pending Payment.
Step 3: The tenant pays. The tenant pays through PayWay in MyBond, through an agency that takes bonds, or at a Service Tasmania shop with the bond number. A prescribed deposit contributor can pay part.
Step 4: Claim at the end. When the tenancy ends, claim the bond in MyBond. The tenant can approve or dispute your claim.
Fee: Maximum bond: Varies: up to 4 weeks' rent
Fee: Lodgement fee: See Consumer Affairs Tasmania
Contact: Rental Deposit Authority and Rental Services: 1300 654 499, rda@justice.tas.gov.au, https://consumeraffairs.tas.gov.au/topics/housing/mybond/owners
Watch out: Never take the bond directly from the tenant: it is illegal in Tasmania.
Watch out: Don't ask for more than 4 weeks' rent, a pet bond, or a higher bond during the tenancy.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register with AICIS before you import or manufacture industrial chemicals (Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme (AICIS)).
If you import or manufacture industrial chemicals for commercial purposes in Australia, including products that contain them such as cosmetics, cleaning products, paints and inks, your business must be registered with the Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme (AICIS) before you introduce them. Registration runs for a registration year from 1 September to 31 August, and introducing chemicals while unregistered is an offence under the Industrial Chemicals Act 2019.
Timeframe: Register online before your first introduction; the 2026-27 registration year runs 1 September 2026 to 31 August 2027, and you renew each year before 1 September. Annual declarations are due by 30 November after each registration year ends.
Cost: For 2026-27 (from 1 September 2026) you pay an A$85 registration fee plus a levy based on the value of chemicals you introduced in the previous financial year. Because of a one-off 90% levy discount, totals range from A$85 (level 1, under A$50,000) to A$3,585 (level 8, A$15 million or more). No GST applies.
Before you start: Work out whether you are an introducer: AICIS says anyone who imports or manufactures industrial chemicals for commercial purposes must register, including businesses, sole traders and individuals, and including people importing products that contain industrial chemicals.
Before you start: Add up the value of the industrial chemicals you imported or manufactured in the previous financial year (for 2026-27 registration, 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026). This sets your registration level. If you are registering for the first time and introduced nothing in that period, you are level 1.
Before you start: Have your business details ready so you can enrol in AICIS Business Services, the online portal used for registration, renewals and declarations.
Before you start: Be ready to categorise every chemical you introduce. Each chemical (including each ingredient in a mixture) must fall into one of five categories: listed, exempted, reported, assessed, or commercial evaluation authorisation. AICIS publishes free decision tools to help.
Before you start: Set up a record-keeping system from day one. AICIS says you must keep records for 5 years, even after you stop introducing the chemical, and provide them within 20 working days if asked (stated for assessed introductions).
Before you start: If you will not introduce industrial chemicals after 31 August, tell AICIS through the 'advise of non-renewal' option in AICIS Business Services rather than just letting registration lapse.
Step 1: Work out your registration level. Use the AICIS registration calculator. Your level is based on the total value of industrial chemicals you imported or manufactured in the previous financial year (1 July to 30 June). The calculator also shows your fee and levy. Level 1 is A$0 to A$49,999 and level 8 is A$15,000,000 or more. (time: Before you register)
Step 2: Enrol in AICIS Business Services. New users create an account in AICIS Business Services, the AICIS online portal. Follow the AICIS guidance on creating an account. Renewing users simply log in. AICIS has tips on usernames and resetting passwords if you are locked out. (form: AICIS Business Services enrolment)
Step 3: Register or renew for the registration year. In AICIS Business Services, open the Registration section and select the registration year (2026-27). Enter your registration level and pay the registration fee and levy. You must be registered before you introduce industrial chemicals on or after 1 September 2026. (time: Before your first introduction in the registration year (registration year starts 1 September); cost: A$85 to A$3,585 for 2026-27 depending on level)
Step 4: Categorise each chemical before you introduce it. For every chemical, decide its category. Listed: already on the Australian Inventory of Industrial Chemicals; meet any listing terms. Exempted: very low risk; no pre-notification, but some need a once-off post-introduction declaration. Reported: low risk; submit a once-off pre-introduction report before you start. Assessed: medium to high risk; you need an assessment certificate (fee applies) before you import or manufacture. Commercial evaluation authorisation: time-limited, for testing commercial viability (fee applies). (time: Before introduction (reported and assessed categories need action before you import); cost: No fee for listed, exempted or reported; fees apply for assessment certificates and commercial evaluation authorisations)
Step 5: Keep records for every introduction. Keep records showing how you categorised each chemical and that you met the category requirements. AICIS says its decision tools are general guidance only and a completed decision tool is not enough on its own to meet your record-keeping obligations. Keep records for 5 years. (time: Ongoing; keep for 5 years)
Step 6: Lodge your annual declaration. After each registration year, declare in AICIS Business Services that the chemicals you introduced were authorised. Submissions open in August. If you introduced nothing, select 'Did not introduce' in the portal. Example from AICIS: introductions between 1 September 2023 and 31 August 2024 had to be declared by 30 November 2024. (time: Due 30 November after the end of each registration year; cost: No fee stated)
Step 7: Renew every year, or tell AICIS you are stopping. Renew in AICIS Business Services for the new registration year before you introduce chemicals on or after 1 September. If you are stopping, use 'advise of non-renewal' for the new year. (time: Before 1 September each year)
Fee: Level 1 registration (A$0 to A$49,999 introduced): A$85.00 (2026-27, from 1 September 2026. Fee only, no levy.)
Fee: Level 2 registration (A$50,000 to A$99,999): A$95.00 (2026-27 total: A$85 fee + A$10 discounted levy)
Fee: Level 3 registration (A$100,000 to A$249,999): A$105.00 (2026-27 total: A$85 fee + A$20 discounted levy)
Fee: Level 4 registration (A$250,000 to A$499,999): A$120.00 (2026-27 total: A$85 fee + A$35 discounted levy)
Fee: Level 5 registration (A$500,000 to A$2,999,999): A$295.00 (2026-27 total: A$85 fee + A$210 discounted levy)
Fee: Level 6 registration (A$3,000,000 to A$4,999,999): A$460.00 (2026-27 total: A$85 fee + A$375 discounted levy)
Fee: Level 7 registration (A$5,000,000 to A$14,999,999): A$2,535.00 (2026-27 total: A$85 fee + A$2,450 discounted levy)
Fee: Level 8 registration (A$15,000,000 or more): A$3,585.00 (2026-27 total: A$85 fee + A$3,500 discounted levy)
Fee: Level 5 registration, previous year for comparison: A$2,180.00 (2025-26 (1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026): A$80 fee + A$2,100 charge. AICIS says levies return to 2025-26 levels, indexed, from 2027-28, so budget for a big rise next year.)
Fee: Level 8 registration, previous year for comparison: A$35,080.00 (2025-26: A$80 fee + A$35,000 charge)
Contact: AICIS: 1800 638 528 or +61 2 8577 8800, https://www.industrialchemicals.gov.au/node/121
Watch out: Introducing an industrial chemical without being registered is an offence under the Industrial Chemicals Act 2019. Register before the goods arrive, not after.
Watch out: Small importers of cosmetics, soaps, cleaning products, fragrances and similar goods often do not realise they are chemical introducers. Importing a product that contains an industrial chemical counts.
Watch out: The 90% levy discount is one-off for 2026-27 only. From 2027-28 levies return to 2025-26 levels with two years of indexation, so a level 5 business that pays A$295 now could pay over A$2,180 next year.
Watch out: Your level is based on the previous financial year's introductions, not your expected sales. Under-declaring your level is a compliance risk.
Watch out: A chemical in the 'assessed' category cannot be imported until you hold an assessment certificate. 'Reported' chemicals need the pre-introduction report lodged before you start.
Watch out: Missing the 30 November annual declaration is a separate compliance failure, even if you are registered. If you imported nothing, you still select 'Did not introduce'.
Watch out: Assessment certificate application fees rose from 1 September 2026 and the certificate application structure changes from 1 July 2027 (five types reduced to three).

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Get therapeutic goods onto the ARTG before you import and sell them (Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)).
Medicines, vitamins and supplements, and medical devices must generally be entered in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) before you can lawfully supply them in Australia. An Australian sponsor applies to the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), pays application fees and annual charges, and takes legal responsibility for the product. Importing for your own personal use is a separate, limited scheme and cannot be used for resale.
Timeframe: Medical devices: the TGA makes its preliminary assessment decision within 20 business days of a paid application, longer if selected for audit. Listed (AUST L) medicines are validated electronically and listed on submission; registered medicines take much longer.
Cost: From 1 July 2026: a listed medicine (AUST L) costs A$1,063 to apply plus A$1,566 a year; a Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring) medical device costs A$651 to apply plus A$121 a year; Class IIa/IIb devices A$1,244 plus A$1,305 a year; Class III A$1,603 plus A$1,662 a year. Audits and registered medicines cost much more.
Before you start: Confirm your product is a therapeutic good at all. Some products are regulated as foods or cosmetics instead, and some goods are excluded or exempt (Schedules 5, 5A and 7 of the Therapeutic Goods Regulations 1990 list product exemptions).
Before you start: Search the ARTG. If the product is already on it, you may be able to buy from the existing sponsor and sell as a retailer instead of becoming a sponsor yourself, though commercial agreements may prevent this.
Before you start: Decide who will be the sponsor. The sponsor is the person or company that supplies the goods in Australia and is legally responsible for them. If you import directly from the manufacturer and are the first point of supply, you need TGA approval as sponsor.
Before you start: For medical devices, get a written agreement with your manufacturer so you can obtain technical information quickly. You must answer TGA information requests within set timeframes and allow inspections.
Before you start: Confirm the manufacturer meets requirements: overseas medicine sites need GMP clearance, and device manufacturers need conformity assessment evidence (for example an overseas certificate the TGA accepts) or a TGA conformity assessment certificate.
Before you start: For listed (AUST L) supplements, check every ingredient is a permitted ingredient and every claim is a permitted indication, and hold evidence for your claims before you list.
Before you start: Budget for ongoing annual charges and post-market duties: adverse event reporting, recalls, advertising code compliance, and keeping records (devices: up to 10 years or the device's lifetime).
Step 1: Create a TGA Business Services (TBS) account and register your organisation. Sponsors and manufacturers must register their details with the TGA before seeking approval. TGA Business Services (also called eBS) is the primary application portal for applications and ongoing compliance. Keep your contact details current.
Step 2: Medical devices: classify the device and submit manufacturer evidence. Work out the device class and category. Certain Class I, Class 1 IVD and export-only devices need only a manufacturer's declaration of conformity with the application. All others need manufacturer evidence (such as conformity assessment certificates) submitted in TBS and accepted by the TGA before you draft the inclusion application. One accepted piece of evidence can support multiple applications.
Step 3: Medical devices: apply for ARTG inclusion and pay. Lodge the inclusion application in TBS. You receive an invoice after submission and the TGA does not review the application until it is paid. Application fees are non-refundable. The TGA aims to make a preliminary assessment decision within 20 business days. Outcomes are approved, selected for audit (extra time and audit fees), or refused. (time: Preliminary decision within 20 business days of payment; cost: A$651 (Class I) to A$1,603 (Class III) application fee; audit fees from A$4,926 if selected)
Step 4: Listed medicines (most vitamins, minerals, herbal supplements): list through the electronic listing facility. Listed complementary medicines can contain only permitted low-risk ingredients and make permitted indications. You apply through the electronic listing facility in TGA eBusiness Services; the application must pass electronic validation, and you certify that the product meets all legal requirements. The TGA does not evaluate the claims before listing, but runs random and targeted compliance reviews. Each listed product gets an AUST L number that must appear on the label. (time: Listed once the application validates and is submitted; cost: A$1,063 application fee and A$1,566 annual charge (from 1 July 2026))
Step 5: Registered medicines: apply for evaluation. Higher-risk products (registered complementary medicines, over-the-counter medicines and prescription medicines) are evaluated before they are entered on the ARTG. Fees depend on the application level (for example OTC N1 to N5, registered complementary RCM1 to RCM5). (cost: From A$2,077 + A$5,133 (OTC N1) upward)
Step 6: Pay annual charges and claim the annual charge exemption if eligible. Annual charges are levied in July each year for every ARTG entry that existed at any time in the financial year. Products entered on or after 1 July 2015 can get an annual charge exemption until they generate turnover. Self-declarations must reach the TGA between 1 July and 22 July each year; late declarations before 15 September cost extra. To avoid next year's charge, ask for cancellation by 30 June. (time: Declarations 1 to 22 July each year; cost: See fees)
Step 7: Meet post-market obligations. Report adverse events, support recalls, follow the Therapeutic Goods Advertising Code, keep information on the ARTG current (lodge variations when things change), and for devices notify the TGA within 60 days if manufacturer evidence is suspended, revoked or lapses. (time: Ongoing)
Fee: Listed medicine (AUST L) application: A$1,063.00 (From 1 July 2026)
Fee: Listed medicine (AUST L) annual charge: A$1,566.00 (From 1 July 2026, per ARTG entry)
Fee: Registered complementary or OTC medicine annual charge: A$2,061.00 (From 1 July 2026)
Fee: OTC medicine N1 application + evaluation: A$7,210.00 (A$2,077 application + A$5,133 evaluation, from 1 July 2026)
Fee: Medical device Class I application: A$651.00 (Includes sterile and measuring Class I; from 1 July 2026)
Fee: Medical device Class I (other) annual charge: A$121.00 (Class I sterile or measuring: A$879)
Fee: Medical device Class IIa or IIb application: A$1,244.00 (Annual charge A$1,305)
Fee: Medical device Class III application: A$1,603.00 (Annual charge A$1,662 (AIMD annual charge also A$1,662))
Fee: IVD medical device application (all classes): A$1,244.00 (Annual charge A$948 (except Class 4 in-house))
Fee: Medical device application audit, Level 1: A$4,926.00 (Level 2 (Class III) A$18,118)
Fee: Late annual charge exemption declaration: A$537.00 (For up to 5 entries, plus A$62 per extra entry, if lodged after 22 July and before 15 September)
Contact: TGA general enquiries: 1800 020 653 (free call) or +61 2 6289 4124, https://www.tga.gov.au/contact-us
Contact: TGA Business Services (eBS) help: 1800 010 624, eBS@health.gov.au, https://www.tga.gov.au/contact-us
Contact: TGA medical devices: 1800 141 144, devices@tga.gov.au, https://www.tga.gov.au/contact-us
Contact: TGA complementary and OTC medicines: nonprescriptionmedicines@health.gov.au, https://www.tga.gov.au/contact-us
Watch out: Supplying therapeutic goods that are not on the ARTG (and not exempt) can attract civil and criminal penalties.
Watch out: The Personal Importation Scheme is for you or your immediate family only. Goods imported under it cannot be sold, supplied or given away. It is not a way to test a market.
Watch out: Personal imports are capped at 3 months' supply per import and 15 months' supply in any 12 months. Prescription-only medicines need a valid Australian prescription at the time of import (eScripts are not accepted).
Watch out: Vaping products, controlled substances and counterfeit medicines or devices cannot be imported under the Personal Importation Scheme. Some herbal or dietary supplements contain controlled ingredients such as ephedra or DHEA that need a permit.
Watch out: Non-compliant imports can be seized and destroyed with no compensation, and fines or legal proceedings may follow.
Watch out: Annual charges apply for every financial year an ARTG entry exists, even if you sold nothing, unless you lodge the exemption declaration between 1 and 22 July. Cancel unwanted entries by 30 June.
Watch out: From 24 July 2026, nicotine pouches cannot lawfully be imported or supplied unless on the ARTG or covered by a statutory exemption pathway.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Equipment licence to import pre-charged refrigeration and air conditioning equipment (National Environmental Protection Agency (National EPA). The licence pages now sit on nationalepa.gov.au; some related pages are still on the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) site.).
If you import refrigeration or air conditioning equipment (including vehicles, boats and other goods with air conditioners) that contains or is designed to use a synthetic greenhouse gas or HCFC refrigerant, you generally need an equipment licence (EQPL) under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act 1989 before you import. The licence costs A$3,000, lasts 2 years, and comes with 6-monthly reporting and a levy on the gas you import.
Timeframe: The National EPA aims to assess a complete application within 2 weeks; the legal maximum is 60 days. Apply before you import.
Cost: A$3,000 non-refundable licence application fee (every 2 years), plus an import levy of A$165 per metric tonne of synthetic greenhouse gas (HCFCs A$3,000 per ozone depleting potential tonne), waived if the total for a reporting period is A$330 or less. You also need membership of an approved product stewardship scheme. No GST.
Before you start: Check if you need a licence at all. Equipment using carbon dioxide (R744), hydrocarbons or ammonia (R717) does not need an EQPL.
Before you start: Small-quantity exemption: you do not need a licence if you import up to 25 kilograms of HFC, PFC, SF6 or NF3 equipment in a calendar year (measured by the gas in the equipment).
Before you start: Personal-use exemption: vehicles or other equipment you have owned for more than 12 months and are importing for your own use may qualify. Email ozone@dcceew.gov.au before you import or pay the fee to check.
Before you start: Check the equipment is not banned. Importing and manufacturing HCFC and CFC refrigeration and air conditioning equipment is banned, with limited exceptions. Air conditioning equipment with a refrigerant charge of 2.6 kg or less is also subject to restrictions under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Regulations 1995.
Before you start: The applicant's legal name must match the Australian Business Register and you need an ABN. A trust cannot hold a licence, so apply in the trustee's name.
Before you start: Join an approved product stewardship scheme before applying. The licence page names Refrigerant Reclaim Australia as the currently approved scheme, and you must attach evidence of membership.
Before you start: Have certified identification for the person signing the application, and a trust deed or partnership authority document if relevant.
Step 1: Confirm whether your goods need an EQPL. Work out what gas the equipment contains or is designed to use and how many kilograms you will import in the calendar year. If it is a natural refrigerant (CO2, hydrocarbon, ammonia) or you stay at 25 kg or less of HFC/PFC/SF6/NF3 equipment, you do not need a licence. If unsure whether your import is equipment or bulk gas, contact the regulator.
Step 2: Join a product stewardship scheme. Get evidence that you are a member of an approved product stewardship scheme (currently Refrigerant Reclaim Australia). You attach it to your application. (time: Before applying; cost: Scheme membership costs not published on the regulator page)

Before you start: Register a BICON account if you need to apply for a permit or want email alerts when a case changes. You need the account to apply for, track and manage permits.
Before you start: Check whether you can meet every condition of a standard permit. If you cannot, you must apply for a non-standard permit, which needs a more detailed risk assessment and takes longer.

Note every document, treatment and permit requirement listed. (time: Same day; cost: Free)
Step 2: Register a BICON account. Create a registered user account in BICON. DAFF offers a 15 minute 'Introduction to BICON' eLearning module and printable task cards in the BICON Help menu. (time: Same day; cost: Free)
Step 3: Apply for the import permit in BICON (if the case says one is needed). Lodge an electronic permit application through BICON. Choose a standard permit only if you can meet all its fixed conditions; otherwise apply for a non-standard permit. Paying does not guarantee a permit. Before you start: Check where the goods were made or shipped from. Measures apply to targeted goods manufactured in or shipped from a target risk country. In 2025-26 these were the USA, Canada and most of Europe plus Russia, Turkey, Ukraine, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Confirm the 2026-27 list on the DAFF BMSB page.
Before you start: Japan, China and the Republic of Korea were heightened vessel surveillance countries (not mandatory cargo treatment) in 2025-26; the UK, China, Japan and Korea were emerging risk countries with random inspection of target goods. Goods made in a target risk country but shipped via another country are still caught.
Before you start: Check the tariff chapter. Target high risk goods (mandatory treatment): chapters 44, 45, 57, 68, 69, 70, 72 to 76, 78 to 89. Target risk goods (random inspection): chapters 27, 28, 29, 38, 39, 40, 48, 49, 56.
Before you start: Check the shipping mode. Break bulk, open top, flat rack and modified containers must be treated offshore. Sealed, six hard-sided containers can be treated offshore or on arrival.

Check the shipping date, country of manufacture and shipment, tariff chapter, and container type against the current season's measures on the DAFF BMSB page and in BICON. Goods outside the listed chapters are exempt unless packed in the same container or consignment as target high risk or target risk goods. (time: Before booking freight)

Offshore treatment in a target risk country must be done by a provider registered under the AusTreat scheme. Onshore treatment is done at approved arrangement sites (classes 12.1 methyl bromide, 12.2 sulfuryl fluoride, 12.3 heat). DAFF recommends offshore treatment, or packing that allows effective onshore treatment, to reduce border delays. (cost: Set by the treatment provider)

In 2025-26, goods treated in a target risk country before 1 December had to be shipped (break bulk) or the container sealed within 120 hours of treatment finishing. Fee: DAFF out-of-office (inspection) fee, ordinary hours: A$70 (Per 15 minutes per person, 2026-27)

Australia bans importing anything containing asbestos, at any level, and the ABF actively targets imported cars and parts. As the owner you must be sure the car contains no asbestos before it ships. If the ABF flags your car you must give evidence; if that is not enough it will direct sampling and testing at the border at your cost, and asbestos parts are seized.
Timeframe: No fixed timeframe. Sort it out in Japan before shipping; a border hold for sampling and testing adds days to weeks of storage and delay.
Cost: No government fee. You pay for any parts replacement, technical evidence, sampling by an independent competent person, NATA-accredited testing, and storage while held.
Before you start: The ban applies to every vehicle regardless of type, age, value or country of origin, and to temporary imports. Japan banning asbestos does not mean a Japanese car is free of it; aftermarket parts are a common source.
Before you start: List the high-risk parts the ABF names: brake pads and shoes, clutch linings, gaskets (cylinder head, extractors, exhaust), seals (fuel tank, mastic, windows), bonnet liners, heater and air conditioner housings, fibrous washers, sound deadening, firewalls, heat shields, wiring wrap, body seam sealers, bituminous coatings and insulation.
Before you start: Decide your assurance route before shipping: technical evidence from the manufacturer that OEM parts are asbestos-free, records of replacing at-risk parts with documented asbestos-free parts, or an accredited test report that clearly links to this specific car and the parts tested.
Before you start: A seller's, supplier's or mechanic's informal statement is not enough evidence. 'Asbestos-free' labels under overseas standards may still allow low levels that are illegal here.
Before you start: Keep every record (work orders, parts invoices, test reports) and make sure they name the VIN or chassis number. The ABF can ask for them at any time.
Step 1: Assess the car's risk. Consider age, make, model, maintenance history and any aftermarket parts. Older cars and cars with replaced brakes, clutches or gaskets are higher risk. Ask your exporter or the selling dealer for service history. (time: Before you buy)
Step 2: Remove or test suspect parts in Japan. The ABF prefers testing or removing suspect parts before shipment, and notes that replacing them may be cheaper than sampling and testing. Keep work records and evidence of the make, model and composition of replacement parts. Overseas sampling and testing must meet Australian laboratory reporting requirements. (time: Before shipping)
Step 3: Make an honest declaration. Only make a 'no asbestos' declaration if you are certain, covering OEM and aftermarket parts and naturally contaminated materials. Your customs broker will ask about asbestos when lodging the import declaration.
Step 4: Respond if the ABF flags the car. If the ABF considers the car at risk, you (or your broker) must give sufficient assurance with documents. If the evidence is not enough, the ABF directs sampling and testing at the border and supervises it while the car is under customs control. (time: Depends on how fast you supply evidence)
Step 5: Arrange sampling and NATA-accredited testing if directed. You must engage a qualified, independent competent person to identify and sample suspect parts; the ABF does not take samples or remove asbestos. Analysis in Australia must be by a NATA-accredited laboratory. Storage costs while waiting are yours whether or not asbestos is found. (time: Days to weeks; cost: You pay sampling, testing and storage)
Step 6: Deal with any positive result. Goods found to contain asbestos are seized and forfeited for disposal. Asbestos parts must be removed under ABF control before the car can be released, and you may face penalties.
Contact: Australian Border Force: 131 881, https://www.abf.gov.au
Contact: Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency: 1300 326 148, enquiries@asbestossafety.gov.au, https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au
Watch out: Zero tolerance: any level of asbestos is prohibited, including chrysotile (white) asbestos, and 'undisturbed' asbestos is not treated as safe.
Watch out: Penalties under the Customs Act: section 233 up to 1,000 penalty units or three times the value of the goods, whichever is greater; section 233BAA up to 1,000 penalty units and/or 5 years' imprisonment; companies up to 5,000 penalty units or 15 times the value. The ABF can also issue infringement notices.
Watch out: All delay, storage, sampling and testing costs fall on you, even if the test comes back clear.
Watch out: Enthusiast car shows do not count as 'display', so you cannot get a permit to import an asbestos-containing car you plan to drive or show.
Watch out: Aftermarket brake pads, clutch kits and gaskets bought cheaply overseas are a common cause of detections.
Watch out: The ABF lists recent detections in imported cars, including a 1971 Mazda RX-2, so older Japanese cars are not exempt.

Before you start: Check the wheels, wheel guards, mud guards, engine bay, underside and chassis rails, boot and spare tyre well, storage compartments, seats and seat folds, vents, and window and door seals.
Before you start: Consider using a recognised offshore cleaning and pre-inspection provider (ROCIP) in Japan. Your car is released only after an import declaration is lodged and duty, GST, any luxury car tax (LCT) and charges are paid. The general duty on passenger cars is 5%, but cars that are Japanese originating goods are duty free under the Japan-Australia Economic Partnership Agreement if you hold valid origin evidence. GST is 10% of the value of the taxable importation, and LCT is 33% of the value above the threshold (A$80,809 in 2026-27).
Timeframe: Lodge the declaration once the car is in transit; release usually follows quickly once approvals, biosecurity and payment are in place.
Cost: Duty 0% (Japanese origin with evidence) or 5%; GST 10% of VoTI; LCT 33% above A$80,809 (A$91,661 fuel-efficient); import processing charge A$152 electronic for values A$10,000 and over; A$71 biosecurity charge; broker fees.
Before you start: Have your import approval number from ROVER. The ABF will not release the car without it.
Before you start: Gather the purchase invoice, auction and payment records, Japanese export or deregistration certificate, bill of lading, freight and insurance invoices, and your ID. Keep all documents for 5 years.
Before you start: Get origin evidence for the JAEPA free rate: a certificate of origin from an authorised body, or an origin certification document completed by the importer, exporter or producer. It must exist when the car is imported and is valid for 12 months from issue. A car built outside Japan (even if sold in Japan) is not Japanese originating.
Before you start: Expect a valuation question for a used car. The ABF says many used vehicles cannot use the price paid, and the usual method is an expert appraisal of the car's value on landing, which you arrange and pay for.
Before you start: Decide whether to use a licensed customs broker (the ABF recommends one for first-time or occasional importers) or lodge yourself through the ICS or on paper at an ABF counter.
Before you start: Check the air-conditioning gas. Cars with HFC-134a (or retrofitted systems holding refrigerant) may need an equipment licence unless the personal use exemption (owned over 12 months, private use) or the low volume exemption (up to 25 kg a year) applies. HFO-1234yf is not regulated. Pre-1996 CFC-12 systems are banned except under the personal use exemption.
Step 1: Engage a licensed customs broker (or get ICS access). Find a licensed customs broker on the ABF list. Give them your ROVER approval, invoice, bill of lading, export certificate, origin evidence, freight and insurance details and asbestos evidence. (time: Before the ship arrives)
Step 2: Classify and value the car. Passenger cars are in tariff heading 8703, with separate statistical codes for used cars by engine type and size. Customs value is normally the transaction value converted to AUD at the exchange rate on the export date; for used cars that were driven before export or depreciated, an appraisal of landed value (fall-back method) is often required. (time: 1 to 5 days)
Step 3: Lodge the import declaration (N10). Required for goods worth over A$1,000. Lodge electronically in the Integrated Cargo System, through a broker, or on paper (form B650 for sea cargo) at an ABF counter. Claim JAEPA preference with scheme code JEPA if the car is Japanese originating and you hold valid origin evidence. (time: Once the car is in transit; form: Form B650 Import declaration (paper lodgement))

Japanese originating goods: Free under Schedule 11 of the Customs Tariff (JAEPA). Without valid origin evidence the 5% general rate applies; you may later claim a refund if you obtain a valid document. (cost: 0% or 5% of customs value)
Step 5: GST is worked out on the value of the taxable importation. VoTI = customs value + duty + international transport and insurance to Australia. GST = 10% of VoTI. GST-registered businesses approved for the ATO deferred GST scheme can defer it to their BAS; duty is still paid before release. (cost: 10% of VoTI)

Private importers pay LCT on entry. The ATO's worked example: LCT value A$101,500 gives ($101,500 - $80,809) x 10/11 x 33% = A$6,207.30. (cost: 33% of value above threshold (x 10/11))

Before you start: Check whether your goods need an export permit, for example agricultural goods (Department of Agriculture), defence and dual-use goods (Defence Export Controls), wildlife (EPBC permits), or other prohibited exports.
